title: Linking verbs: be, appear, seem; become, get, etc.

sections.title: Linking verbs: what they are
sections.content:
When an adjective or noun phrase is used after a verb to describe the subject or say what or who the subject is, the adjective or noun phrase is a complement and the verb is a linking verb:
• Clara is a doctor.     My cat's getting old.     She seemed unable to concentrate.
Other linking verbs fall into three groups:
• 'being' linking verbs: e.g. be, keep, prove, remain, stay — Most of these verbs can be followed by either an adjective or noun phrase (e.g. It sounds nice / a nice place).
• 'becoming' linking verbs: e.g. become, come, end up, get, grow, turn out — When they are used as linking verbs, come and grow (e.g. come to know, grow thoughtful) can't be followed by a noun phrase.
• 'seeming' linking verbs: e.g. appear, look, seem, sound — Keep is only followed by a noun if an adjective follows it (e.g. It kept him awake).

sections.title: Appear, look, prove, seem, turn out: optional "to be"
sections.content:
After the verbs appear (= seems true), look (= seem), prove, seem, and turn out we can often either include or omit to be:
• The room appears (to be) brighter than when I last saw it.
However, following these verbs to be is usually included before the adjectives alive, alone, asleep, and awake, and before the -ing forms of verbs:
• I didn't go in because she appeared to be asleep. (not … she appeared asleep.)
Before a noun we include to be when the noun tells us what the subject is, but often leave it out when we give our opinion of the person or thing in the subject. We leave out to be in formal English. Compare:
• He walked into what seemed to be a cave. (not … what seemed a cave.) and
• She seems (to be) a very efficient salesperson.

sections.title: Become, get, grow: processes of change
sections.content:
We use the linking verb become to describe a process of change. A number of other linking verbs can be used instead of become, including come, get, go, grow, turn (into).
We use get rather than become: in informal speech and writing before some adjectives including difficult, ill, interested, pregnant, and worried; in imperatives; and in phrases such as get changed (clothes), get dressed, get married / divorced:
• I first got suspicious when he looked into all the cars. (more formally … became suspicious…)
We prefer become for a more abstract or technical process of change:
• He became recognised as an expert.
• Their bodies have become adapted to high altitudes.
We use become, not get, if there is a noun phrase after the linking verb:
• Dr Morales became an adviser to the government.
Also with: apparent, aware, convinced, infected, irrelevant, obvious

sections.title: Go, turn: colour changes and unwanted situations
sections.content:
We use go or turn, not usually get or become, when we talk about colours changing:
• The traffic lights turned / went green and I pulled away.
We often use go to talk about changes, particularly for unwanted situations. For example:
go deaf / blind / bald; go mad / crazy / wild; go bad / off / mouldy / rotten; go bust; go dead; go missing; go wrong. But note: get ill, get old, get tired.
• The company went bust and had to close.
• My computer's gone wrong again.
• Some people get ill very easily.
After the verbs come, get, and grow (but not after become) we can use a to-infinitive. Come and grow are often used to talk about gradual change:
• I eventually came / grew to appreciate his work. (not … became to appreciate his work.)

exercises.question: The job turned out to be far easier than I'd expected.
options: turned out (to be) far easier — 'to be' can be omitted
exercises.hint: After 'turn out', 'to be' can often be left out before an adjective.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: turned out (to be) far easier — 'to be' can be omitted
Turn out and prove are linking verbs that describe how a situation was eventually found to be. They are followed by a complement (adjective or to-infinitive) and are used in both formal and informal contexts. Turn out is more informal; prove is more formal.

exercises.question: When I looked through the window, Ella appeared to be alone.
options: appeared to be alone — 'to be' should be KEPT (adjective 'alone')
exercises.hint: Before 'alone', 'to be' is usually included after 'appear'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: appeared to be alone — 'to be' should be KEPT (adjective 'alone')
Before 'alone', 'to be' is usually included after 'appear'.

exercises.question: What he called his 'little cottage in the country' proved to be a castle.
options: proved to be a castle — 'to be' should be KEPT (noun = what the subject is)
proved (to be) a castle — can omit
exercises.hint: Before a noun telling us what the subject IS, include 'to be'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: proved to be a castle — 'to be' should be KEPT (noun = what the subject is)
Turn out and prove are linking verbs that describe how a situation was eventually found to be. They are followed by a complement (adjective or to-infinitive) and are used in both formal and informal contexts. Turn out is more informal; prove is more formal.

exercises.sentence: The soup tastes sourly — I think you added too much lemon.
exercises.correction: The soup tastes sour — I think you added too much lemon.
exercises.hint: Linking verbs (taste, smell, look, feel, sound) are followed by adjectives, not adverbs.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: tastes sour
Linking verbs connect the subject to a describing word. After linking verbs (taste, smell, look, feel, seem, become, appear), use an ADJECTIVE (sour, tired, happy), not an adverb (sourly, tiredly, happily). The adjective describes the SUBJECT, not the action.

exercises.question: Hassan proved to be an excellent source of information about the town.
options: proved (to be) an excellent source — 'to be' can be left out (opinion)
exercises.hint: Giving an opinion about the person — 'to be' optional; also in formal English leave it out.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: proved (to be) an excellent source — 'to be' can be left out (opinion)
Turn out and prove are linking verbs that describe how a situation was eventually found to be. They are followed by a complement (adjective or to-infinitive) and are used in both formal and informal contexts. Turn out is more informal; prove is more formal.

exercises.question: I've adjusted the aerial and the television seems to be working okay now.
options: seems to be working — 'to be' must be KEPT (before -ing form)
exercises.hint: Before -ing forms of verbs, 'to be' is usually included.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: seems to be working — 'to be' must be KEPT (before -ing form)
Before -ing forms of verbs, 'to be' is usually included. This verb pattern requires a gerund (-ing form) as its object.

exercises.question: He only looked to be about ten years old, but I knew he must be a lot older.
options: looked (to be) about ten years old — 'to be' can be omitted
exercises.hint: After 'look', 'to be' is often optional.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: looked (to be) about ten years old — 'to be' can be omitted
After 'look', 'to be' is often optional. Linking verbs connect the subject to a complement (adjective or noun phrase) that describes the subject. They do not describe an action — they describe a state or change of state.

exercises.sentence: She became very happily after hearing the news about her promotion.
exercises.correction: She became very happy after hearing the news about her promotion.
exercises.hint: 'Become' is a linking verb — use an adjective, not an adverb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: became very happy
'Become' is a linking verb of change — it is followed by an adjective describing the new state: 'became angry', 'became clear', 'became available'. Using an adverb ('happily') is wrong because adverbs describe how an action is done, not what a subject is.

exercises.question: I was at a zoo once when an elephant ___ and attacked its keeper. (go / turn)
exercises.hint: Unwanted situation / strange behaviour → go (went berserk).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: went berserk (unwanted situation → go)
Unwanted situation / strange behaviour → go (went berserk).

exercises.question: A few seconds later, the line ___ and Marc put down the handset. (go / turn)
options: went bust (phone/signal going dead → go bust/dead)
exercises.hint: Phone line going silent → 'went dead' (unwanted situation → go).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: went dead
Phone line going silent → 'went dead' (unwanted situation → go).

exercises.question: After the spider bit Rachel, her ankle ___ and started to swell up. (go / get)
options: went red / turned red (colour change → go or turn)
exercises.hint: Colour change (ankle going red) → turned red or went red both work.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: turned red (turn)
Colour change (ankle going red) → turned red or went red both work.

exercises.question: After the storm the sea ___ (grow) very calm within an hour.
exercises.hint: 'Grow' as a linking verb = gradually become → past simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: grew
'Grow' as a linking verb means to gradually become. It is followed by an adjective: 'grow calm', 'grow impatient', 'grow cold'. This is a process-of-change verb, like 'become', 'get', 'turn'. Use the past simple for a completed process.

exercises.question: He's actually quite friendly when you ___ him.
options: get to like / come to like (gradual process → come/get + to-infinitive)
Both get to like and come/grow to like
exercises.hint: Gradual change → come/get/grow to like (not become to like).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both get to like and come/grow to like
Gradual change → come/get/grow to like (not become to like).

exercises.question: I'll take over driving when you ___ tired.
options: get tired (adjective: tired → use get, not go)
exercises.hint: 'Get tired' is the fixed collocation (not go tired).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: get tired (adjective: tired → use get, not go)
'Get tired' is the fixed collocation (not go tired).

exercises.question: We soon ___ each other and have been great friends ever since. (become / come)
options: Both came to know and got to know
exercises.hint: Gradual process of getting to know → come to know or get to know.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both came to know and got to know
Gradual process of getting to know → come to know or get to know.

exercises.question: The milk ___ (go) sour because we left it out overnight.
exercises.hint: 'Go + adjective' describes an unwanted change of state.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: went
'Go' as a linking verb typically describes unwanted or undesirable changes: go sour, go bad, go wrong, go bankrupt, go mad. It is always followed by an adjective. Use the past simple for a completed change.

exercises.question: Blog: '(1) everything seemed to turn wrong' → Correction?
options: seemed to go wrong (go wrong = fixed idiom)
exercises.hint: 'Go wrong' is the fixed collocation, not 'turn wrong'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: seemed to go wrong (go wrong = fixed idiom)
'Go wrong' is the fixed collocation, not 'turn wrong'.

exercises.question: Blog: '(5) hadn't become dressed' → Correction?
options: hadn't got dressed (get dressed = fixed phrase)
exercises.hint: 'Get dressed' is the fixed phrase for putting on clothes.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: hadn't got dressed (get dressed = fixed phrase)
'Get dressed' is the fixed phrase for putting on clothes.

exercises.question: Blog: '(7) got missing' → Correction?
exercises.hint: 'Go missing' is the fixed idiom — not 'get missing'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: gone missing (go missing = fixed idiom)
'Go missing' is the fixed idiom — not 'get missing'.

exercises.question: Blog: '(8) to become worried' → Correction?
options: to get worried (informal → get, not become, with 'worried')
exercises.hint: Informal speech + 'worried' → get worried (not become worried).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: to get worried (informal → get, not become, with 'worried')
Informal speech + 'worried' → get worried (not become worried).
